subject: Connectivity options for Acme Analytics private deployment: VPC peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN

Subject: Connectivity options for Acme private deployment: VPC peering / PrivateLink / S2S VPN

Hi Sam / Priya,

Thanks again for the time yesterday. Attached are the two artifacts I promised: a network diagram that overlays the possible connectivity patterns and a short spreadsheet that scores VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints / AWS PrivateLink), and site-to-site IPsec VPN against your requirements (latency, egress IP control, auditability, and ops overhead).

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- VPC peering: 
  - Pros: lowest hop-count and predictable latency for intra-region traffic, native routing, minimal per-request overhead.
  - Cons: cross-account routing semantics, limited to same region (unless you use inter-region peering), harder to restrict path to only the inference control plane (requires careful subnet/NACL/route table work).
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints):
  - Pros: explicit service endpoint, fine-grained access control (security groups), avoids transitive routing concerns, easier to expose a single service endpoint for egress IP stability when combined with NAT.
  - Cons: additional ENI management, per-GB data processing costs on some clouds, slight added hop and potential throughput limits if not sized correctly.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec):
  - Pros: works for on-prem and cloud-to-cloud, simple for customers with strict network boundaries, can provide explicit egress IPs at the customer gateway.
  - Cons: higher latency variance, key rotation and tunnel reliability considerations, and more operational burden for both sides vs. PrivateLink.

Our recommendation for the pilot (based on your stated constraints: sub-50ms p95 inference path, strict auditing, and wanting a single ingress endpoint for multiple accounts) is to pilot PrivateLink for the control/data plane with an IPsec S2S VPN fallback for on-prem failover or regions where PrivateLink is not available.

Ask: can we schedule a 45-minute runbook/ops call tomorrow to align on NAT egress expectations and whether your infra team prefers us to host the NAT (so egress IP is stable from Redwood) or rely on your egress appliances?

Attached: acme_mcp_network_diagram.png, private-deploy-transport-comparison.xlsx

Thanks,

Thanks Jasmine — useful summary. A couple quick clarifications from our side: 
1) Egress IPs are important because our security team needs a stable allowlist for downstream telemetry and third-party services. If PrivateLink still requires us to manage NAT on our side, that is fine; we just need that to be stable.
2) Throughput: some of our peak inference bursts are expected to be large (hundreds of MBs/sec). Can PrivateLink handle sustained throughput at that scale without per-ENI throttling?

We can do the runbook/ops call tomorrow at 10:00am PT. Priya and I will bring a network engineer to talk about IPs and throughput constraints.

—Sam

Jasmine — quick engineering note for the ops call tomorrow, copied Jordan for visibility:

Short checklist and recommended defaults for the pilot:
- Default: PrivateLink interface endpoint exposed from Redwood-managed account per-region; Acme configures SGs to allow the service ENI. That gives us the clean auth boundary and reduces cross-account route complexity.
- NAT / Egress: if Acme wants a stable egress IP for third parties, they can host a single NAT gateway in their account and route PrivateLink outbound traffic through it. Alternatively, Redwood can offer egress proxies (we already do that for a subset of enterprise pilots) — tradeoff is we add an extra operational step and egress cost.
- Throughput: PrivateLink scales by adding more ENIs / endpoint network interfaces and distributing connections; with our traffic patterns we recommend at least 4 ENIs initially and autoscaling based on network metrics. We'll validate in the pilot.
- Failover pattern: configure primary PrivateLink, and a second S2S IPsec tunnel to Redwood edge for cross-region fallback and on-prem short-circuits. Use health checks and route priorities for automatic failover.
- Audit/logging: endpoint flow logs + VPC Flow Logs aggregated into the same Splunk/Datadog workspace works well; Redwood can push connection metadata to your audit pipeline if you prefer an integration.

I'll have slides prepped with the pilot config and a short MoSCoW (must/should/could) list. Jordan — if this looks like the right direction I can convert to a mutual action plan (MAP) and get signatures.

Ben

Sam / Priya — thanks for the quick call. Short recap and agreed next steps (we'll attach the signed MAP request once we have internal approvals):

Recap / decision for pilot:
- Pilot connectivity: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) as primary ingress for control + data plane, with Redwood-managed S2S IPsec tunnels as a documented fallback for on-prem and cross-region traffic.
- Egress: Acme will host a dedicated NAT gateway in their account to provide stable egress IPs to downstream partners. Redwood will document required route/nat rules and test from staging.
- Throughput: start pilot with 4 ENIs for the PrivateLink endpoint; Redwood will monitor throughput and add ENIs if we observe saturation.
- Observability: enable VPC Flow Logs and endpoint flow logs; Redwood will add connection-level metrics to the MAP for the first 2 weeks.

Next actions and owners:
- Acme (Sam/Priya): provide the intended NAT egress IP and preferred PoP region by EOD Monday (2026-07-05).
- Redwood (Ben/Jasmine): produce the MAP and pilot runbook and share DocuSign link.
- Scheduling: test window targeted week of 2026-07-12; Redwood to provide a staging checklist by 2026-07-07.

Attachments: mutual-action-plan.docx (draft attached).

I'll follow up with the DocuSign link and a short packet for your network team. Thanks all — look forward to the pilot.
